- [A 900,000 Beer-can Mardi Gras](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966/1966-03-26-a-900-000-beer-can-mardi-gras/) — Moomba's eleventh year comes into its own as a genuine street festival, with a parade crowd estimated at 900,000 along Swanston Street, an anti-Vietnam demonstration that pelted television host Graham Kennedy with flour, and the customary carpet of empty beer cans along the Yarra banks.
- [Sulks in the Bedroom](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966/1966-04-02-sulks-in-the-bedroom/) — Pat Phoenix, who plays Elsie Tanner in Coronation Street, visits Melbourne on a personal appearance tour and reflects on the programme's grip on its audience, from fans threatening her sailor boyfriend to strangers who left memorial wreaths when Mrs Barlow was killed off.
- [The Mighty Wurlitzer Rose in a Pool of Light.](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966/the-mighty-wurlitzer-rose-in-a-pool-of-light/) — A visit to the Regent Theatre's Mighty Wurlitzer organ, one of only two left working in Australia, and a morning practice session with virtuoso organist Tony Fenelon.
- [The Phantom Rolls-Royce](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966/1966-04-16-the-phantom-rolls-royce/) — The Melbourne City Council orders a Phantom V Rolls-Royce for the Lord Mayor at $23,800, prompting a survey of the Council's peculiar anachronisms, from the Civic Group's gentlemanly rotation of the mayoralty to the ongoing failure to build a civic square or make sensible use of a city block opposite Myer.
- [Who's Been Working on the Railroad?](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966/1966-04-30-whos-been-working-on-the-railroad/) — Melbourne's underground railway dream traces a 40-year history of reports, promises, shelved starts and lottery schemes, from the 1929 Metropolitan Town Planning Commission report through the Utah Construction Company's flat offer to build in three years, to the Wilbur Smith and Associates study of 1966 that recommends the same underground the city has been talking about since 1925.
- [The Wall Street End of Collins Street](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966/1966-05-07-the-wall-street-end-of-collins-street/) — A lament for the retail and architectural decline of Collins Street's eastern end, as banks and insurance houses squeeze out old shops and new high-rise buildings obliterate the old paving stones, lamps, and Victorian facades.
- [The Battle of the Sly Bakers: 90,000 Illegal Loaves](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966/1966-05-14-the-battle-of-the-sly-bakers-90000-illegal-loaves/) — Melbourne's long-running underground war over illegal weekend bread baking, where 90,000 families buy fresh loaves from clandestine Sunday bakeries while union officials and the Trades Hall Council condemn the practice as sweated labour in unsanitary conditions.
- [The Dancing Girls of Little Lon](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966/1966-05-21-the-dancing-girls-of-little-lon/) — An interview with ballerina Kathleen Gorham at her new dance academy in Little Lonsdale Street, where she reflects on her twenty-year career with the Borovansky Ballet and Australian Ballet, her admiration for Robert Helpmann and Margot Fonteyn, and her decision to retire from performance.
- [Preparing for an Invasion](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966/1966-05-28-preparing-for-an-invasion/) — The Batman television craze hits Melbourne, as American promoter Alex Tolmer arrives to sell the 1960s TV phenomenon to Australian networks, with the show having already generated $5 million in royalties and 500 licensed Batman products from shaving cream to ice-cream.
- [The Great Football Fade-out](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966/1966-06-11-the-great-football-fade-out/) — A statistical and cultural argument that Melbourne's claim to be the world's greatest football city is overstated, with crowd figures failing to keep pace with population growth and a large section of the community only going through the motions of football devotion.
- [Everything in Apple-Pie Order](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966/1966-06-18-everything-in-apple-pie-order/) — A tour of Appletree Hill, a new outer-Melbourne housing estate designed entirely by architect Robin Boyd, where every house, garden, fence and toolshed follows his modernist principles, raising the question of whether living beautifully in Boyd's mould leaves room for a treehouse or a boat.
- [Flying Ladies and Rich Young Men](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966/1966-06-25-flying-ladies-and-rich-young-men/) — The eighth National Rally of the Rolls-Royce Owners' Club descends on Canberra with 101 cars, from pristine 1909 Silver Ghosts to the latest Silver Shadow, and Keith Dunstan discovers why collectors who already own four or five see no reason to stop.
- [Another Encore for the Square Dance](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966/1966-07-02-another-encore-for-the-square-dance/) — Melbourne's 110-year obsession with building a civic square is traced through a parade of proposals, from an 1856 newspaper leader and a Jubilee scheme tied to Parliament House, through post-war plans to demolish the Windsor Hotel and Princess Theatre, to the current stand-off with the English Hammerson development group over the Swanston and Collins Streets corner site.
- [Hitting the Clubs on the Head](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966/1966-07-09-hitting-the-clubs-on-the-head/) — Melbourne's private clubs face a crisis following the end of six o'clock closing, with the Hardware Club, University Club, Royal Caledonian Club and Public Schools Club all shedding members or contemplating moves, while the Yorick Club debates whether to merge with the Savage Club or simply wind up, and the boom business shifts to a carpet-lined hotel in Hawthorn with a Breathalyser at the bar.
- [Moses and the Monash Red Sea](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966/1966-07-16-moses-and-the-monash-red-sea/) — Charlton Heston visits Melbourne on a U.S. State Department goodwill tour, plays exhibition tennis against Frank Sedgman at Grace Park as a Bethesda Hospital fund-raiser, and gives poetry readings at Monash University and other venues, finishing with Robert Frost's 'Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening', which he had read on a TV memorial program two days after President Kennedy's assassination.
- [Swinging Little Englanders](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966/1966-07-23-swinging-little-englanders/) — Two young British debaters on a Commonwealth Relations Office universities tour argue that the twentieth century is a cultural catastrophe, pitching swinging London against American mass culture and Pop Art, while a Melbourne audience votes the motion down 200 to 71, reassured by a student's observations on the creative forces of Picasso, James Joyce and Henry Moore.
- [Among the Pasties](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966/1966-07-30-among-the-pasties/) — A tour of Sydney's King's Cross strip clubs, from the Pink Pussy Cat to the Crazy Horse, appraising the performers, the audiences and the bizarre economics of a world where a good stripper earns seventy pounds a week and can appear at three clubs a night.
- [Wanted, a Civic Symbol](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966/1966-08-06-wanted-a-civic-symbol/) — The case for Melbourne's proposed Lower Yarra bridge as the city's long-missing civic symbol, with a detailed comparison of its planned dimensions against the Sydney Harbour Bridge and a sidelight on the Rebecca Riots as a precedent for toll-gate fury.
- [Conquering the Impossible Cowlick](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966/1966-08-13-conquering-the-impossible-cowlick/) — A tour of Melbourne's male grooming revolution, from the Aramis fragrance counter at Georges to the new unisex hairdressing salons, as barber shops discover cologne, skin cream and the concept of the male toiletry barmaid.
- [A Beautiful Blending of Blues](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966/1966-08-20-a-beautiful-blending-of-blues/) — The launch of the Men's Fashion Council's Australian Fashion Express tour, a train fitted out to spread the gospel of conservative dressing through the four eastern states, reported from Spencer Street with a wary eye on the matching Paisley cufflinks.
- [Queuing for the Grand Final](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966/1966-08-27-queuing-for-the-grand-final/) — The annual ritual of camping outside the MCG for football grand final tickets, chronicling the culture of canvas-town camaraderie, the absurdity of the regulations banning it, and the irony of the queue moving from the ground to the clubs.
- [A Really Fantastic Queue](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966/1966-09-24-a-really-fantastic-queue/) — Dr Leon Mann of Melbourne University's Psychology Department analyses the behaviour of VFL grand final ticket queues, explaining why people stay past the point where they know they have no hope of getting in, through wish-fulfilment and wounded pride.
- [A Marvellous Auction Sale](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966/1966-10-01-a-marvellous-auction-sale/) — A charity auction for Melbourne's Cultural Centre raises funds through improbable lots, LBJ's hat, Patrick White's autographed plays, Dita Cobb's false eyelashes, while the centre itself remains mired in a naming dispute between 'National Gallery and Art Centre of Victoria' and the simpler 'Artorium'.
- [Melbourne Cup Winners: Horses or Hats?](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/walkabout-magazine/1966/melbourne-cup-winners-horses-or-hats/) — A survey of the Melbourne Cup as spectacle as much as sport, from Jean Shrimpton's mini-skirted 1965 Derby appearance and the ritual of Cup Day toppers and fashion parades to the race's history, Carbine's 1890 record run, and Archer's 550-mile walk to Flemington in 1861.
- [It Never Rains in the Mallee](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966/1966-10-08-it-never-rains-in-the-mallee/) — The opening of Australia's first full-scale Folk Museum at Swan Hill, built around the restored paddlesteamer Gem and a growing collection of Mallee farming machinery, with Sir Henry Bolte presiding over a sodden ceremony that proved the museum's name something of a misnomer.
- [A Place for Mr. Whippy](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966/1966-10-15-a-place-for-mr-whippy/) — Myer's new $18 million Northland shopping centre opens in Melbourne's north, drawing 150,000 people on its first Tuesday and prompting a tour of its air-conditioned malls, waterless plastic fountain, bistro, gallery paintings and a Mr. Whippy ice cream van finally given a respectable home.
- [Where Is the Eye of Monique?](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966/1966-10-22-where-is-the-eye-of-monique/) — The Bureau of Meteorology's system for naming cyclones, explained through the man responsible for choosing 100 female names every three years, with a history tracing the practice from Brisbane's cantankerous nineteenth-century meteorologist Clement Wragge to the 1966-67 season's lineup of Angela, Colette, Monique and Odette.
- [The Four Days of President Johnson in Australia](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966/1966-10-29-the-four-days-of-president-johnson-in-australia/) — An eyewitness account of Lyndon B. Johnson's 1966 Australian visit, riding in the White House Press Gallery motorcade from Canberra airport and observing a presidential performance that put Australian political oratory to shame, while demonstrators outside the Rex Hotel held signs and protesters tore up placards.
- [In the Wake of the Shrimp](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966/1966-11-05-in-the-wake-of-the-shrimp/) — The 1966 Melbourne Cup Fashions in the Field contest, which pitted Dupont's model Jean Shrimpton against Wool's Baroness Fiona Thyssen, and Dunstan's interview with the Baroness about her life as a newly separated working model.
- [Which City is in Front...?](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966/1966-11-12-which-city-is-in-front/) — A survey of the Melbourne versus Sydney rivalry, examining competing newspaper claims about population growth, migration, new industries, building completions and personal income, prompted by the CIA-level precision with which LBJ's visit was split equally between the two cities.
- [Courage, Not to Stumble, Brother](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966/1966-11-19-courage-not-to-stumble-brother/) — The history of Victoria's beer monopoly under Carlton and United Breweries, and the arrival of the Courage Brewery of England with plans for a $11 million Melbourne plant, raising the question of whether hotelkeepers will dare switch allegiances.
- [Getting into Troubled Waters](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966/1966-11-26-getting-into-troubled-waters/) — The long history of the Victoria-South Australia border dispute, from the 1839 survey through successive High Court and Privy Council cases to the 1966 standoff over offshore oil rights, with Sir Henry Bolte threatening a blockade of Corio whisky and Melbourne Cup horses.
- [1966 and All That](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/walkabout-magazine/1966/1966-and-all-that/) — A tongue-in-cheek review of 1966, the year of decimal currency, Robert Menzies' retirement and Harold Holt's spear-fishing bikini photographs, the Pentridge escape of Ronald Ryan, conscription protests, the mini-skirt, and Lyndon Johnson's visit to Australia.
- [One Must Take a Stand](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966/1966-12-03-one-must-take-a-stand/) — The Melbourne Cricket Ground's history from its elegant colonial origins to the current demolition of the Grey Smith Stand and the Snake Pit bar, as a new $2.5 million three-tier stand is built to lift capacity to 122,000 and outrace the VFL's competing stadium at Waverley.
- [The Ways of a Greyfriars Man](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966/1966-12-10-the-ways-of-a-greyfriars-man/) — The enduring appeal of Billy Bunter and the Greyfriars school fiction of Frank Richards, whose 1966 holiday annual and school prospectus revealed a world of fagging, tuck shops and earnest house rules still finding eager readers among a certain generation of Melbourne book buyers.
- [Lost a Dragon, Gained a Tower](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966/1966-12-17-lost-a-dragon-gained-a-tower/) — The demolition of the St. James building at the corner of Bourke and William Streets, and the AMP Society's plans for a 37-storey office tower on the site, designed by the San Francisco firm Skidmore, Owings and Merrill and destined to be Melbourne's tallest building, albeit twelve feet shorter than its Sydney counterpart.
- [In a State over Hanging](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966/1966-12-24-in-a-state-over-hanging/) — Victoria's troubled history with capital punishment, from the 1951 triple execution of Jean Lee, Norman Andrews and Robert Clayton to the 1962 Robert Peter Tait case, and the imminent hanging of Ronald Ryan for the murder of prison warder George Hodson, with Premier Sir Henry Bolte refusing all deputations or reprieve.
- [The End of a Pressure Group](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1966/1966-12-31-the-end-of-a-pressure-group/) — Melbourne's hydraulic lift system, sentenced to close on 31 December 1966 after a 1962 pipe burst and a successful compensation claim, is mourned in a farewell visit to the City Council power house in Spencer Street, where the superintendent evokes eighty years of hydraulic history from the wool presses at the docks to the Regent Theatre's rising organ console.
- [The Napoleon Solo Caper](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967/1967-01-07-the-napoleon-solo-caper/) — A lunch at the John Batman Motor Inn with Robert Vaughn, the American actor playing Napoleon Solo in "The Man from U.N.C.L.E.", who held court on Vietnam, Kennedy politics, and the impossibility of crossing from television to film.
- [Times Past at Lorne](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967/1967-01-28-times-past-at-lorne/) — A return visit to the Lorne holiday resort on Victoria's surf coast, comparing its genteel 1906 reputation with the folksingers, coffee lounges, and renovated Pacific Hotel of 1967, with a nostalgic glance across the bay at the superior tone claimed by Portsea.
- [Protesting as a Way of Life](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967/1967-02-04-protesting-as-a-way-of-life/) — An interview with David Nadel, Monash Labor Club president and organiser of the Anti-Ky demonstration, on how Melbourne's protest movement works, from the organisation of marches to the legal strategy of passive resistance.
- [A Rare and Beautiful Occasion](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967/1967-02-11-a-rare-and-beautiful-occasion/) — Keith Dunstan attends the 90th anniversary race meeting at Great Western, where champagne at sixpence a glass, spirited betting, a Fashions in the Field contest judged by a pin-up model, and a tour of Seppelts' underground cellars make a gloriously eccentric Victorian country race day.
- [Has Anyone Here Seen Kelly?](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967/1967-02-18-has-anyone-here-seen-kelly/) — Melbourne's Lord Mayor launches a $10,000 fly-control quiz competition, prompting Keith Dunstan to revisit the city's long war against blowflies through the writings of William Kelly, whose 1853 account of Melbourne's plague of flies remains the most vivid on record.
- [Meeting a White Hunter from the N.T.](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967/1967-02-25-meeting-a-white-hunter-from-the-nt/) — A profile of Allan Stewart, former Black Watch lieutenant turned safari camp operator at Nourlangie in Arnhem Land, who runs big-game hunting for clients including Stirling Moss and Reg Ansett while cohabiting with buffalo herds, crocodiles, and memories of thirty days in Fanny Bay gaol.
- [Selling us Short on Derby Day](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967/1967-03-04-selling-us-short-on-derby-day/) — A campaign for shorts as a legitimate Melbourne summer uniform, tracing the saga of a tram conductor suspended for reporting for duty in white shorts, the Tramways Union's failed push for cooler uniforms, and the eccentric history of the garment Australians gave to the world.
- [Where do we go for our Blue Ribbon Security?](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967/1967-03-11-where-do-we-go-for-our-blue-ribbon-security/) — The Victoria Coffee Palace's decision to seek a liquor licence marks the end of Melbourne's last great temperance hotel, prompting a survey of the coffee palace movement's rise and fall from James Munro's 1880 crusade to stripping clubs, executive bus trips to Sydney, and the creeping normalisation of alcohol in the city.
- [This is a fine state to be in](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967-03-18-this-is-a-fine-state-to-be-in/) — A survey of the deteriorating relations between Victoria and New South Wales, arguing Melbourne's case for its rightful place in the international air network via the new Tullamarine airport.
- [This is a fine state to be in](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967/batmans-melbourne-this-is-a-fine-state-to-be-in/) — A survey of the deteriorating relations between Victoria and New South Wales, arguing Melbourne's case for its rightful place in the international air network via the new Tullamarine airport.
- [Morley's Moomba: a king for all occasions](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967/1967-03-25-morleys-moomba-a-king-for-all-occasions/) — English actor Robert Morley reigns as King of Moomba, dispensing caustic one-liners about Melbourne's streets, Flinders Street Station, and marching girls while accompanying Queen Patsy Ann Earp through the Moomba procession and losing enthusiastically at the Bendigo races.
- [A detour to Rutherglen's festival](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967/1967-04-01-a-detour-to-rutherglens-festival/) — A report on the first Rutherglen Wine Festival, where 15 local vineyards discovered that the word "alcohol" could draw crowds from 200 miles away, complete with a wine auction, a float parade, a Saturday night barbecue dispensing wine from pluto taps, and the liquor laws getting in the way of Sunday fun.
- [Doing the right thing by Ned](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967/1967-04-08-doing-the-right-thing-by-ned/) — A report on a Kelly school held in Wangaratta by the Adult Education Centre, where historians Manning Clark, Weston Bate, and Ian Jones assembled to debate Ned Kelly's legal case, military ambitions, and the possibility of a posthumous pardon from Monash University.
- [Alas, poor Tivoli, I knew it well.](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967/alas-poor-tivoli-i-knew-it-well/) — A eulogy for Melbourne's fire-gutted Tivoli Theatre, tracing its history back to the 1850s diggers' Varieties Music Hall through Harry Rickard's opulent 1901 rebuild and its parade of stars from Marie Lloyd to Harry Houdini.
- [Taking the row out of rowing](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967/1967-04-22-taking-the-row-out-of-rowing/) — The centenary Head of the River race on the Barwon traces how school rowing went from a grand social occasion of flour bombs, dunked coxes, and triumphant theatre nights to a tightly regulated event policed by three foolscap pages of Scotch College instructions, with Scotch winning in 1967 just as they had in 1868.
- [The unending wars of the planesmen](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967/1967-04-29-the-unending-wars-of-the-planesmen/) — A blow-by-blow account of the rival publicity battles between TAA and Ansett-ANA over the simultaneous arrival of their first DC9 jets in Melbourne, a rerun of the 1964 Boeing 727 toss-and-tactics war, from competing tarmac ceremonies to a champagne press breakfast and a contest over which airline could claim the most historically travelled passenger.
- [Art on a pastoral binge: wine, food, and fantasy](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967/1967-05-06-art-on-a-pastoral-binge-wine-food-and-fantasy/) — A tour of the gallery movement sweeping Victoria's provincial towns, from the Hamilton Shaw Collection to Ballarat's hotbed of Lindsays and the new Mildura Arts Centre, where the third Mildura Prize for Sculpture drew a washing-machine agitator with a Ford Thunderbird tail-light and a taxi driver who reckoned the winner was two giraffes mating.
- [Here's, perhaps, another place for a future village](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967/1967-05-13-heres-perhaps-another-place-for-a-future-village/) — The case for Westernport Bay as Melbourne's future industrial port, measuring the bay's natural advantages against Port Phillip's treacherous entrance and Corsair Rock, as BP's new Crib Point refinery, a coming Esso oil refinery, and John Lysaght's steel works promise to transform the area.
- [Here's, perhaps, another place for a future village](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967/heres-perhaps-another-place-for-a-future-village/) — A case for Westernport Bay as Victoria's great industrial port of the future, tracing the historical accident that gave Melbourne Port Phillip over the far superior Westernport and surveying the refineries, steelworks and soaring land prices already transforming the Hastings shoreline.
- [Met any good, used football players lately?](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967/1967-05-20-met-any-good-used-football-players-lately/) — A comic proposal to apply used-car-lot logic to the VFL's open transfer market, prompted by the $8000 purchase of Hawthorn full-forward Peter Hudson from New Norfolk and the collapse of the Coulter Law against buying and selling players.
- [Met any good, used football players lately?](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967/met-any-good-used-football-players-lately/) — A survey of the collapse of the Coulter Law's genteel fiction that footballers cannot be bought and sold, tracing the season's transfer fees from country leagues to the VFL and proposing a Used Footballer Lot along the Nepean Highway where buyers could inspect cartilages and check ear counts.
- [As conspicuous as a negro at a KKK picnic](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967/1967-05-27-as-conspicuous-as-a-negro-at-a-kkk-picnic/) — A report from the Melbourne concerts of Little Stevie Wonder, whose extraordinary stage presence reduced a 7,000-strong teenage crowd to mass hysteria while Keith Dunstan stood out rather conspicuously as the only adult male among the screaming fans.
- [As conspicuous as a negro at a KKK picnic](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967/as-conspicuous-as-a-negro-at-a-kkk-picnic/) — Keith Dunstan reports on Little Stevie Wonder's Australian tour, tracing the pandemonium of 7000 fans at a Sydney concert where police, security men and ambulance officers struggled to contain girls aged 14 to 17 fainting, weeping and tearing at their own hair, and contrasting the hysteria with the singer's composed, almost supernatural stage presence.
- [The straightest furrow in the west](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967/1967-06-03-the-straightest-furrow-in-the-west/) — A dispatch from the World Ploughing Championships at Wangaratta, where 17 nations competed in tracksuits and Tyrolean hats for the most exquisitely turned third of an acre, amid the competing din of five demonstration chain-saws.
- [The straightest furrow in the west](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967/the-straightest-furrow-in-the-west/) — A report on the World Ploughing Championships held near Wangaratta, where representatives of 17 nations in Olympic blazers competed over a third of an acre each, Keith Dunstan finding the contest as soporific as Test cricket but discovering an unexpected tension in the twiddle of tappets and the measurement of furrows with a ruler.
- [The last touch to the business of the soft sell](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967/1967-06-10-the-last-touch-to-the-business-of-the-soft-sell/) — A brochure from the Melbourne Crematorium at Fawkner prompts a history of cremation in Victoria, from the illicit 1895 beach bonfire at Sandringham to the slow respectability won by the Cremation Society through the 1920s.
- [The other Edinburgh (Part one of two parts)](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967/1967-06-10-the-other-edinburgh-part-one/) — The centenary of Prince Alfred's 1867 Australian tour passes unremarked, prompting a retelling of the extraordinary colonial welcome he received in Melbourne, culminating in the disastrous Citizens' Free Banquet in Richmond Park where 60,000 descended on provisions for 10,000 and the wine flowed literally into the street.
- [For Wally Hoysted, the whips are well and truly out](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967/1967-06-17-for-wally-hoysted-the-whips-are-well-and-truly-out/) — A portrait of Walter Hoysted, the solitary Melbourne anti-flogging campaigner who parks a furniture van outside Flemington cataloguing the number of times each horse is struck, challenges jockeys to take 20 strokes on the bare back for charity, and has been to jail for his trouble.
- [The other Edinburgh (Part two of two parts)](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967/1967-06-17-the-other-edinburgh-part-two/) — The second part of the centenary retelling of Prince Alfred's 1867 Australian tour: the shooting of the Duke at Clontarf by Henry O'Farrell, the wave of anti-Irish feeling it unleashed across the colonies, O'Farrell's trial and execution, and HMS Galatea's quiet departure.
- [A poser: what to do with a million dead marines?](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967/1967-06-24-a-poser-what-to-do-with-a-million-dead-marines/) — The rise of the no-return bottle threatens the bottle-oh, the Methodist Boy Scouts and the garbage men's European holiday funds, as the Bottle Merchants' Association and the soft-drink makers go to war over who owns Australia's empties.
- [Psychedelic underpants give a man assurance](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967/1967-07-01-psychedelic-underpants-give-a-man-assurance/) — Frank Eidlitz opens Melbourne's first psychedelic discotheque, the Ginza in Little Bourke Street, with six projectors throwing swirling images across dancers and ceiling while Keith Dunstan reports feeling merely queasy.
- [By day the loafers, at night the scoundrels](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967/1967-07-15-by-day-the-loafers-at-night-the-scoundrels/) — A centenary tribute to Melbourne's General Post Office, tracing its nine-year construction from 1859, its grand opening on Victoria's separation day weekend, and the "Argus" reviewer who warned its colonnade would be a paradise for loafers by day and scoundrels by night.
- [The sporting way to get rid of those messy crowds](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967/1967-07-22-the-sporting-way-to-get-rid-of-those-messy-crowds/) — A satirical proposal to abolish live sporting crowds entirely, replacing spectators with television coverage and piped crowd noise, saving clubs the expense of grandstands and parking while converting sports grounds into landscaped parks.
- [It's a tough job now keeping up with the Joneses](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967/1967-07-29-its-a-tough-job-now-keeping-up-with-the-joneses/) — Melbourne detective Barry Jones becomes the father of quadruplets, prompting reflections on the fertility drug gonadatrophin, the contraceptive pill's impact on Australia's birth rate, and a colonial-era account of a Warrnambool woman who gave birth to sextuplets in 1841.
- [Even 'Rock-Fist Rogan' couldn't win this one](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967/1967-08-05-even-rock-fist-rogan-couldnt-win-this-one/) — A campaign to amalgamate Melbourne's suburban councils into a Greater Melbourne authority founders against entrenched local resistance, with even a figurative street fighter unable to land a blow on the city's fragmented municipal politics.
- [Apres le ski it's the Tyrolean mini-skirts](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967/1967-08-19-apres-le-ski-its-the-tyrolean-mini-skirts/) — A field report from Falls Creek, where Victoria's ski fields are reinventing themselves with carpetbag steaks, wine lists and Tyrolean-costumed waitresses in a bid to match the plush reputation of New South Wales resorts like Thredbo.
- [For men only, and everything so discreet](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967/1967-08-26-for-men-only-and-everything-so-discreet/) — A visit to Melbourne's first executive men's hairdressing salon, where hairpieces, tinting, permanents and facials are dispensed with the utmost discretion to businessmen who would rather not be seen to care about their appearance.
- [Nothing like the good old Carlton love-ins](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967/1967-09-02-nothing-like-the-good-old-carlton-love-ins/) — Melbourne's first hippie 'love-in' at Carlton's Love Centre draws a correspondent who finds young innocents in hired antique uniforms, psychedelic music, and a brisk trade in Iron Cross medals and Bob Dylan posters, with the hippie movement's second-hand military chic its most surprising feature.
- [They're high, wide, handsome and available](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967/1967-09-09-theyre-high-wide-handsome-and-available/) — Melbourne's office building boom has produced towers with prestige address plaques and embarrassingly empty floors, as the city discovers it cannot breed white-collar workers fast enough to fill the marble palaces rising across the CBD.
- [Where there's a Pill there's a way to get Leslie to Wesley](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967/1967-09-16-where-theres-a-pill-theres-a-way-to-get-leslie-to-wesley/) — The centenary history of Wesley College, written by Geoffrey Blainey and others, offers a frank account of headmaster scandals, flogging controversies and the school's transition from fee-starved colonial beginnings to producing Menzies and Holt, prompted by a fifth-form boy's letter to the school magazine about hooliganism in the corridors.
- [Lady Luck's favors are a real lottery](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967/1967-09-23-lady-lucks-favors-are-a-real-lottery/) — Tattersall's raises its ticket price to 60 cents and lifts the first prize to $25,000 in a lottery war against Queensland and New South Wales, while the story of how the sweep was driven from state to state by moral outrage before finding refuge in Tasmania illuminates both the gambling instinct and the wowser tradition.
- [Talking Turkey and a little Gaelic about football](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967/1967-09-30-talking-turkey-and-a-little-gaelic-about-football/) — The MCG's spectacular new western stand, with its cantilever overhangs, beer reticulation system and a scoreboard 115 feet above street level, is completed just in time for the finals, while Ron Barassi prepares to take a team to Dublin despite a Gaelic Athletic Association rule book that threatens suspension for anyone who plays or even attends cricket.
- [Home bottling goes down the drain](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967/1967-10-07-home-bottling-goes-down-the-drain/) — A fond elegy for Melbourne's home wine-bottling culture, tracing the pleasures of bulk barrels, siphons and improvised cellars as rising wine prices and shrinking supply begin to kill the tradition off.
- [No more bed and board for our Cliveden set](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967/1967-10-14-no-more-bed-and-board-for-our-cliveden-set/) — A history of Cliveden Mansions in East Melbourne, the grand apartment hotel built in 1887 by Sir William Clarke, tracing its rise as a resort of the colonial gentry and its long decline into an era of plastic flowers and electric rooftop signs.
- [The risks of tending phlox by night](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967/1967-10-21-the-risks-of-tending-phlox-by-night/) — Melbourne's worst drought in recorded history brings severe water restrictions, prompting a flood of inventive conservation measures from readers and a warning from the Board of Works that 360 plain-clothes inspectors are watching for illegal sprinkler use.
- [PMG knocks the mystique out of S.E.2](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967/1967-11-04-pmg-knocks-the-mystique-out-of-s-e-2/) — South Yarra's surge as Melbourne's swingingest suburb at the expense of fading Toorak, whose grand estates have been subdivided away and whose prestige postal code S.E.2 has been wiped out by the Postmaster-General's switch to four-digit numbers.
- [A cry in agony: 'Save the parking meters!'](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967/1967-11-11-a-cry-in-agony-save-the-parking-meters/) — A visit to Surfers Paradise finds the beach half-rebuilt after the storm that threatened to topple Garfield Towers into the surf, the Progress Association's Meter Maids still feeding sixpences into parking meters, and the new Mayor Bruce Small opening rotary conventions in lion cages and conducting the Salvation Army Band as a man of quite extraordinary civic energy.
- [Some imported fillies just aren't stayers](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967/1967-11-18-some-imported-fillies-just-arent-stayers/) — A wry account of the Melbourne Cup's "Fashions in the Field" contest, the VRC's escalating quest for celebrity imports, and the diplomatic furore when Princess Soraya of Persia scratched at the last minute due to a dispute over transport and rising times.
- [Nowhere for a refined person to hang his hat](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967/1967-11-25-nowhere-for-a-refined-person-to-hang-his-hat/) — A lament for Melbourne's vanishing grand hotels and coffee palaces, as the Palace Hotel and Menzies Hotel face demolition to make way for new office towers, depriving the city of the establishments where Trollope, Paderewski and Dame Nellie Melba once stayed.
- [What is hatching at the sign of the golden cockerel](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967/1967-12-02-what-is-hatching-at-the-sign-of-the-golden-cockerel/) — A behind-the-scenes look at the brewing battle about to reshape Victoria, as British Courage Brewery readies its new Broadmeadows plant to challenge Carlton and United Breweries' long monopoly, with lavish press lunches, masked taste tests, and talk of two-tap hotels.
- [Around the turn and straight into the red](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967/1967-12-09-around-the-turn-and-straight-into-the-red/) — A detailed account of the financial crisis gripping Victoria's major racing clubs, with the VRC carrying an overdraft of $849,000 and the VATC similarly stricken, and the fierce political battle over mid-week racing and the threatened closure of Cranbourne, Werribee and Yarra Glen.
- [The art of upmanship among the joggers](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967/1967-12-16-the-art-of-upmanship-among-the-joggers/) — A sardonic guide to the jogging craze sweeping Melbourne, from the competitive fibbing about distances run to the precise art of wearing a suitably battered track-suit, as middle-aged men driven by coronary anxiety thrash themselves around Caulfield racetrack before dawn.
- [The war on want strides painfully ahead](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967/1967-12-23-the-war-on-want-strides-painfully-ahead/) — A vivid account of Melbourne's sponsored walk fundraising craze, culminating in the 20-mile "Walk Against Want" to Dandenong in which more than 1200 people, including Jim Cairns, Barry Jones and a woman in high heels, raised nearly $18,000 for community aid abroad while covering themselves in blisters.
- [The Ghost of the Princess](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1967/the-ghost-of-the-princess/) — Tells the story of Federici, the Princess Theatre's baritone ghost who collapsed and died on stage playing Mephistopheles in 1888, and the book launch that tried, and failed, to lure his spirit out with themed cocktails.
- [A Place in the Sun — Brown Bros., Milawa](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/the-sun-news-pictorial/1968/1968-01-01-a-place-in-the-sun-brown-bros-milawa/) — Keith Dunstan attends the opening of a new underground cellar at Brown Bros., Milawa, months after a November frost wiped out the vintage, and watches John Brown seal a cache of wines under concrete to be dug up on 1 January 2001.
- [The Bikini, What Next?](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/walkabout-magazine/1968/the-bikini-what-next/) — A history of Australia's long, losing battle to regulate what beachgoers wear and when they may swim, from the segregated sea baths and bathing machines of the 1890s and William Gocher's 1902 defiance of Manly's bathing laws to the 1968 furore over the bikini.
- ["Gawd, couldn't you go a couple of jugs!"](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1968/1968-01-06-gawd-couldnt-you-go-a-couple-of-jugs/) — A visit to Beechworth, the perfectly preserved gold-rush town in north-east Victoria, where the annual Golden Horseshoes Festival re-enacts an 1873 Chinese procession with elaborate costumes, Tom Mitchell on horseback, and a time capsule buried beneath the town hall steps.
- [A green lawn is the badge of shame](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1968/1968-02-10-a-green-lawn-is-the-badge-of-shame/) — Melbourne's severe drought of early 1968 turned garden watering into a civic crime, with the Board of Works running water patrols and neighbours dobbing each other in at the rate of fifty cases a day, while an Aboriginal rainmaking team from the Moorawarri tribe was flown down from back of Bourke by a plastic raincoat company.
- [Giving play to no end of vicious proclivities](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1968/1968-02-17-giving-play-to-no-end-of-vicious-proclivities/) — Victoria's new permission for Sunday sport-for-profit from March 1968 prompts Keith Dunstan to survey a century of Melbourne's magnificent Sabbatarian battles, from the army's Sunday gun salute in 1855, through the Chloe scandal at the National Gallery, to the city's brief, perfect era of absolutely nothing happening on a Sunday.
- [An elegy for seven elms](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1968/1968-02-24-an-elegy-for-seven-elms/) — The Melbourne City Council's pre-dawn felling of seven 80-year-old elms in St Kilda Road, to give the RSL an uninterrupted view of the Shrine of Remembrance, provokes Keith Dunstan to survey a century of Melbourne's passionate, litigious and occasionally joyful tree controversies.
- [Secrets of the No Doubt Clinch](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1968/1968-03-02-secrets-of-the-no-doubt-clinch/) — Keith Dunstan reproduces a door-to-door encyclopaedia salesman's complete word-for-word script, including stage directions, pauses, and the final 'No Doubt Clinch' manoeuvre, then wonders which Melbourne Jones family the company has in its promotional sights.
- [The cultural benefits of a really good row](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1968/1968-03-09-the-cultural-benefits-of-a-really-good-row/) — The National Gallery of Victoria's imminent move into its new Roy Grounds-designed St Kilda Road building is reported from the inside, including a 3 a.m. security operation to transfer 200,000 pieces, a jaded Venus with her broken belongings in a bag, and Phar Lap presiding imperiously over it all in the McCoy Hall.
- [Paying homage to our national drink](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1968/1968-03-16-paying-homage-to-our-national-drink/) — Keith Dunstan attends the Beer Appreciation Society of Australia's first beer festival at Templestowe, where members in special regalia taste six masked stubbies through a formal tasting sheet, Carlton products dominate every one of the six samples, and the gentlemanly quest continues to acquire Young and Jackson's Hotel as an official BASA pub.
- [All well bibbed and bibbing well](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1968/1968-03-23-all-well-bibbed-and-bibbing-well/) — Keith Dunstan reports from the second Rutherglen wine festival, where crowds descended despite severe drought and frost cutting the vintage by 75 per cent, bibs and souvenir glasses ran out on the first day, and 10,000 people gatecrashed a starlight barbecue to share stainless-steel barrels of wine pumped through pluto taps.
- [Strange signals and stranger explanations](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1968/1968-03-30-strange-signals-and-stranger-explanations/) — A Venusian visitor stationed in the Fitzroy Gardens writes home to his father explaining Melbourne's baffling customs, from citizens pouring water on dust-covered ground at night to a political class trading baroque insults, culminating in the observation that the planet is clearly doomed and rescue is urgently required.
- [The Year of Anti-Football Protest](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/walkabout-magazine/1968/the-year-of-anti-football-protest/) — Keith Dunstan's account of founding the Anti-Football League in 1967 with Douglas Wilkie, from the badge sold for the Berry Street Babies Home to the posthumous Wilkie Medal awarded to Prime Minister Harold Holt for never once being seen at a match.
- [The great old boys of South Boorook](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1968/1968-04-06-the-great-old-boys-of-south-boorook/) — Jim Allen's annual Hereford cattle sale at his South Boorook property in the Western District, where elaborate facilities rival the Melbourne Royal and a drought-year record of $172,050 for 75 beasts draws buyers from Queensland rather than the stricken district.
- [Paying the price of too much freeloading](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1968/1968-04-13-paying-the-price-of-too-much-freeloading/) — The exhausting proliferation of Melbourne's expense-account PR lunches, from Chilean wine tastings and witchetty grubs to fox meat served by Jacob Van Raalte of Ralta Ltd. in a bid to publicise his non-stick frypan.
- [The possum capital of the world](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1968/1968-04-20-the-possum-capital-of-the-world/) — Melbourne's status as the unofficial possum capital of the world, where protected possums plague well-heeled suburbs from Toorak to Kew, and professional possum-catcher Herbert Tippett of Clifton Hill explains the futile cycle of trapping and releasing them across the Yarra.
- [A tax on virtuous abstainers](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1968/1968-04-27-a-tax-on-virtuous-abstainers/) — A tongue-in-cheek proposal for an Abstainer's Act to tax non-drinkers, non-smokers, non-gamblers and non-motorists, who currently contribute nothing to public revenue from Victoria's TAB, liquor taxes and lottery while decent citizens fund hospitals and the war effort through their vices.
- [One more week](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1968/1968-04-27-one-more-week/) — A weekly news-roundup column touching on the Western Australian by-election, revenue figures from the TAB, racing, tobacco and liquor taxes, and the fiscal paradox of the virtuous abstainer who contributes nothing to public revenue.
- [How to cheat at wine tastings](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/the-australian-gourmet/1968/how-to-cheat-at-wine-tastings/) — A tongue-in-cheek guide to bluffing your way through a masked-bottle wine tasting, from reading cork brands and capsule colours to timing your "hint of crushed violets" line for maximum effect.
- [Loosening the ties of conformity](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1968/1968-05-04-loosening-the-ties-of-conformity/) — Melbourne's necktie as the symbol of civic respectability comes under threat from Lord Snowdon, Harry Miller's pink skivvy at the Tosca opening night, and a Myer advertisement for turtle-neck evening shirts with zips up the back, prompting alarm about what tielessness might mean for the social order.
- [The oddities never got a look in](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1968/1968-05-11-the-oddities-never-got-a-look-in/) — A review of a lavish new coffee-table book on Melbourne with photographs by Gordon De'Lisle and text by Osmar White, which Keith Dunstan praises for its pictures while arguing it pulls its punches on the city's conformism, its lack of an underground railway, its egocentric football culture, and the ugliness of its sprawling suburbs.
- [Adelaide's barmaid drought of sixty years is over](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1968/1968-05-25-adelaides-barmaid-drought-of-sixty-years-is-over/) — South Australia's sixty-year ban on barmaids, driven by temperance societies and King O'Malley's 1896 anti-barmaid campaign, came to an end in October 1967 under Premier Donald Dunstan's new Licensing Act, though Keith Dunstan finds the women at the Arkaba Hotel's Beachcomber Bar wearing grass skirts and flowered bras in a manner that vindicates O'Malley's worst fears.
- ["Darling, I love you," cried the bald bishop](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1968/1968-06-01-darling-i-love-you-cried-the-bald-bishop/) — A report on Melbourne's unlikely religious ferment after a mock crucifixion at Monash University sparked letters columns, TV debates and a student-press god-assembly-kit, culminating in Bishop Howell Witt's disarmingly enthusiastic endorsement of the whole affair.
- [Catering for football's teetotallers](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1968/1968-06-08-catering-for-footballs-teetotallers/) — The Melbourne Cricket Ground's experiment with a no-liquor zone covering three grandstand levels prompts Keith Dunstan to trace the long tradition of drinking at Victorian football, argue the case for a dedicated drinkers' stand, and note Australian Rules football's quietly declining attendances.
- [It's harder than ever to judge a book by its cover](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1968/1968-06-15-its-harder-than-ever-to-judge-a-book-by-its-cover/) — Victorian censorship chief Arthur Rylah's hissing reception at the Melbourne Film Festival inspires Keith Dunstan to celebrate the art of the book blurb, cataloguing the raciest specimens from Harold Robbins, Iris Murdoch and the Elizabethan Trust's own opera brochure.
- [Listening to the cricket isn't what it used to be](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1968/1968-06-22-listening-to-the-cricket-isnt-what-it-used-to-be/) — Keith Dunstan falls asleep during an Ashes broadcast and recalls the lost golden age of Australian cricket radio, from Charlie Moses's wooden-bat sound effects and synthetic broadcasts to the beer-and-crayfish vigils of the Depression-era suburbs.
- [Even death comes duty free](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1968/1968-07-06-even-death-comes-duty-free/) — Keith Dunstan reports from Norfolk Island, a Pacific speck of 1000 people and no taxes that draws 8000 duty-free loot-hunters a year, tracing its convict history, its Norfolk pine forests, its precarious freighter unloading by longboat, and the bitter divide between those who want to preserve it and those who want to develop it.
- [Operation Gold Coast does the trick](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1968/1968-07-13-operation-gold-coast-does-the-trick/) — Bruce Small's audacious Melbourne publicity blitz for Surfers Paradise, bussing meter maids, bikini girls and media teams into the city during miserable winter weather, delivers a 50 per cent booking surge for Ansett-ANA and a front-page picture of a shivering Geri Engleton in a bikini at Swanston and Flinders.
- [Calling on tweenagers to protest](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1968/1968-07-20-calling-on-tweenagers-to-protest/) — Goaded by a discotheque bouncer who calls him grandpa, Keith Dunstan proposes a new social category, the tweenager, for the forgotten generation of forty-somethings squeezed between the politically active pensioners and the news-hogging young, and drafts a platform including ground-length skirts at the Melbourne Cup and madrigals on electric harpsichords.
- [The complete answer to frigidity](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1968/1968-07-27-the-complete-answer-to-frigidity/) — A drive between Sydney and Adelaide through motel country finds Keith Dunstan wrestling with a power-point shortage in the age of the electric blanket, prompting an investigation into a 700,000-unit-a-year boom and the twin-control model's supposed power to save marriages.
- [Dermot-itis](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1968/1968-08-03-dermot-itis/) — A review of Dermot Morrah's royal biography 'To Be a King', in which Keith Dunstan reflects on covering Prince Charles's Australian tour and finds the book's apologetic, over-managed portrait of the Prince no better than the old Crawfie style.
- [Nobody could paint cows better than Scheltema](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1968/1968-08-03-nobody-could-paint-cows-better-than-scheltema/) — A portrait of Melbourne art dealer Julian Sterling and the booming market for Australian paintings, from a $700 Norman Lindsay to $20,000 Drysdales, with a tour of the Heidelberg School artists now fetching serious prices.
- [The weatherman's tip on the ideal climate](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1968/1968-08-10-the-weathermans-tip-on-the-ideal-climate/) — A visit to Melbourne's Bureau of Meteorology reveals the city is second-windiest, second-coldest and has the least sunshine of any Australian capital, yet hosts one of three world meteorological centres, newly equipped with a $1.9 million computer.
- [Isn't it time to bury the Ashes?](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1968/1968-08-17-isnt-it-time-to-bury-the-ashes/) — A frustrated argument for reform of Test cricket between Australia and England, after a series of three draws in 1968, with former captains Ian Johnson and Lindsay Hassett diagnosing the slow over rate as the root cause of unfinished matches.
- [The whole place reeks with atmosphere](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1968/1968-08-17-the-whole-place-reeks-with-atmosphere/) — Melbourne restaurants and pubs compete furiously on atmosphere in 1968, from Dame Zara Holt opening the Lazar with oysters and champagne at breakfast, to the salvaged treasures of Cliveden Mansions headed for the new Dillingham hotel, and Louis Fleyfel's half-million-dollar Le Chateau rising behind a Queensway Road facade.
- [Loyalty that opens cheque books and office doors](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1968/1968-08-24-loyalty-that-opens-cheque-books-and-office-doors/) — A review of John McLaren's book 'Our Troubled Schools' examines Melbourne's public-school pecking order, from Geelong Grammar at the top for the landed aristocracy through to junior technical school students at the bottom, and the intolerable dilemma facing parents over where to educate their children.
- ["Henry's two-bob sideshow" built to last 10,000 years](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1968/1968-08-31-henrys-two-bob-sideshow-built-to-last-10000-years/) — The opening of Melbourne's National Gallery of Victoria on St Kilda Road, with its Leonard French glass ceiling, George Dreyfus fanfare and champagne banquet for 450 guests, prompts Keith Dunstan to declare it the most beautiful gallery he has seen and the city's first genuine tourist symbol.
- [Off-loading your rubbish post haste](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1968/1968-09-07-off-loading-your-rubbish-post-haste/) — A satirical look at a proposed gadget combining a letterbox with a rubbish bin, prompted by the PMG's new push into bulk direct-mail advertising and the flood of junk mail reaching every Australian household.
- [One more week](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1968/1968-09-07-one-more-week/) — A Melbourne arts round-up taking in the National Gallery of Victoria's new building and its first temporary exhibition, a Jawaharlal Nehru memorial at Sydney's Australia Square, Brisbane's new Sunday entertainment laws, and filmmaker John Heyer's latest attempt to raise money for an Australian feature film.
- [The golden promise of the great southland](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1968/1968-09-14-the-golden-promise-of-the-great-southland/) — A report on the opening of Myer's vast new Southland shopping centre on the Nepean Highway, drawing comparisons between Myer's suburban retail empire and Communist state planning, and noting the opening-day chaos of 150,000 shoppers.
- [The continuing sanctification of Mr. Kelly](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1968/1968-09-21-the-continuing-sanctification-of-mr-kelly/) — A survey of the booming Ned Kelly industry in 1968, covering two new books, the launch party at the old Melbourne Gaol, Tourist Bureau tours, commercial merchandise, and three newly discovered letters from Kelly to the Governor of Victoria written in the days before his hanging.
- [The Monkees getting all socially significant](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1968/1968-09-28-the-monkees-getting-all-socially-significant/) — A report on the Monkees' arrival in Melbourne, comparing it to previous airport arrivals from Johnnie Ray, Frank Sinatra and the Beatles, and recounting the band members' surprisingly forthright views on Vietnam, race, police brutality and anarchy at their press conference.
- [Beef Boom in Tombstone Territory](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/walkabout-magazine/1968/beef-boom-in-tombstone-territory/) — A tour of American-financed cattle stations on Cape York Peninsula, where Sir William Gunn's Gunn Rural Management and the King Ranch operation at Tully were fencing scrubmaster herds, breeding Brahmans and Santa Gertrudis, and bulldozing rainforest for legume pasture.
- [The big sell for the big spenders](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1968/1968-10-05-the-big-sell-for-the-big-spenders/) — An account of Australia's campaign to win the 1971 American Society of Travel Agents convention for Sydney, including the Australian Tourist Commission's hospitality suite in San Juan, complete with cocktails named after Australian icons and 160 dozen bottles of Fosters Lager.
- [The long walk back gets even longer](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1968/1968-10-12-the-long-walk-back-gets-even-longer/) — A report on the newly expanded Melbourne Cricket Ground, now capable of holding 124,000, and the 1968 VFL Grand Final between Carlton and Essendon, with observations on declining season attendances and a history of the MCG's slowest cricket innings.
- [A swallow of courage, and one or two more, to christen the brew](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1968/1968-10-19-a-swallow-of-courage-and-one-or-two-more-to-christen-the-brew/) — A report on the opening of Courage's new $8 million brewery at Broadmeadows, Melbourne, including the military-style convoy of 25 red-and-gold trucks up Swanston Street and the ceremonial press launch at which the Beer Appreciation Society rated the new lager lighter and paler than Carlton.
- [A unique dullness that's worth fighting for](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1968/1968-10-26-a-unique-dullness-thats-worth-fighting-for/) — A spirited defence of cricket's glacial pace against calls to brighten the game, drawing on the slowest innings in MCG history and arguing that dull cricket is the ideal tranquilliser in an age of electric parking meters and instant mash.
- [The style of Lord Casey](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1968/1968-11-02-the-style-of-lord-casey/) — A profile of Lord Casey at 78, examining how Australia's Governor-General brought unusual vigour, subtlety and a vast political education to a vice-regal role he treated as a genuine working brief seven days a week.
- [When high-rise really means 'skyscraper'](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1968/1968-11-02-when-high-rise-really-means-skyscraper/) — A tour of the Housing Commission's ambitious new tower blocks rising over South Melbourne, Prahran and Carlton, questioning the social consequences of high-density living while marvelling at the views from the 28th floor.
- [A great country for wowsers](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1968/1968-11-09-a-great-country-for-wowsers/) — An excerpt from Keith Dunstan's new book 'Wowsers', tracing the history of puritanism in Australia from its non-conformist church origins through the temperance movement, coffee palaces and Sabbatarian campaigns to the slow crumbling of wowserism in the 1960s.
- [In the dark the Arcadian revels really got going](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1968/1968-11-09-in-the-dark-the-arcadian-revels-really-got-going/) — A report on Melbourne's arcade revival, from the Royal Arcade's centenary celebrations to the chaotic, blackout-hit reopening of the Centreway arcade in Chapel Street as the Gallery, a wine-and-cheese venue where the lights failed for most of the night.
- [The competing attractions of horseflesh and sheilaflesh](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1968/1968-11-16-the-competing-attractions-of-horseflesh-and-sheilaflesh/) — A sardonic account of the 1968 Melbourne Cup carnival at Flemington, where the assembled international beauties, society girls and the members' car park threatened to eclipse the actual race entirely, with Rain Lover winning in the end.
- [Ruthless competition in the nostalgia trade](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1968/1968-11-23-ruthless-competition-in-the-nostalgia-trade/) — A survey of Victoria's booming heritage preservation movement, from the renovation of Melbourne pubs to Swan Hill's Folk Museum, the Castlemaine Market restoration appeal, and Ballarat's Sovereign Hill gold-mining town project.
- [Getting all steamed-up over diseasels](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1968/1968-11-30-getting-all-steamed-up-over-diseasels/) — Sixty-five American railway enthusiasts from the Pacific Coast Chapter of the Railway and Historical Society visit Melbourne to see its steam locomotives and trams, declaring the Australian Railway Museum at Newport the best they had ever seen and riding Puffing Billy to Emerald.
- [Venturing deep into Sydney safari country](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1968/1968-12-07-venturing-deep-into-sydney-safari-country/) — A visit to the African Lion Safari at Warragamba Dam near Sydney, where 51 lions roam 100 acres, visitors drive their own cars through the paddocks, and a lioness named Wilma puts her head through the car window.
- [Talking of the sad news with Menzies' magnificent ladies](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1968/1968-12-14-talking-of-the-sad-news-with-menzies-magnificent-ladies/) — A farewell to Menzies Hotel in Melbourne, which closes after Christmas and goes to auction in March, told through a conversation with the hotel's two topless figurines Phoebe and Prudence, who recall distinguished guests from Anthony Trollope to Richard Nixon.
- [A good time at the old 'Gabba](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1968/1968-12-21-a-good-time-at-the-old-gabba/) — A report from the first Brisbane Test between Australia and the West Indies, including the historic first Sunday of Test play in Australia, the Cannery Row bar culture of the outer, and performances from Clive Lloyd, Ian Chappell and Ray Lindwall's successor Alan Connolly.
- [Again, It's Time for Change in the Name of Charity](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1969/1969-01-04-batman-s-melbourne-again-its-time-for-change-in-the-name-of-charity/) — Keith Dunstan reports on the Melbourne walkathon from the city to Frankston, a 25-mile endurance march that raised $50,000 for charity through the cunning sadism of sponsor-per-mile pledges, as limping walkers including Herb Elliott stumbled into the Frankston Life Saving Club at 3 a.m.
- [All the Rich Scents of the Bush Rodeo](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1969/1969-01-11-batman-s-melbourne-all-the-rich-scents-of-the-bush-rodeo/) — Keith Dunstan reports from the Myrtleford Rodeo at the foot of Mount Buffalo, where professional roughriders earning $2000 to $5000 a year fracture their bones with cheerful indifference, and the standard events of bareback riding, bulldogging and calf-roping draw bush crowds that never come to the city shows.
- [At Last, the Dance Is Over at St. Kilda](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1969/1969-01-18-batman-s-melbourne-at-last-the-dance-is-over-at-st-kilda/) — The burning of the St. Kilda Palais de Danse at Christmas prompts a history of Melbourne's famous dance hall, from its controversial opening in 1913, when 700 protesters condemned the tango as inflaming animal passions, through the great American bands of the twenties and the eventual reign of wedding receptions and Miss Australia presentations.
- [What's His Is Hers and Vice Versa](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1969/1969-02-08-batman-s-melbourne-whats-his-is-hers-and-vice-versa/) — Keith Dunstan investigates Melbourne's bisexual fashion revolution at the Myer In Gear shop in Lonsdale Street, where boys buy girls' clothes and girls buy boys' clothes, Nehru jackets and cufflinks are interchangeable, and the only reliable way to tell the sexes apart is by hair length.
- [The Leisure Rat-Race Is Merciless](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1969/1969-02-15-batman-s-melbourne-the-leisure-rat-race-is-merciless/) — Keith Dunstan's theory that automation and the do-it-yourself movement are inseparable, the more technology does for us, the more we exhaust ourselves laying our own floor tiles, papering our own walls, and pouring our own concrete, developed after five weeks' holidays left him paint-stained and chisel-scarred.
- [A Visit to Beef Up the Japan Tourist Trade](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1969/1969-02-22-batman-s-melbourne-a-visit-to-beef-up-the-japan-tourist-trade/) — The Australian Tourist Commission brings three Sumo wrestlers to Australia, led by grand champion Taiho, who earns $100,000 a year and at six-foot-three and 316 pounds demolishes a banquet at the Sukiyaki Restaurant in Alfred Place with methodical dignity, buying koala bears and boomerangs before departing for home.
- [The Wedding, the Greatest Thing Since the Bogle Case](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1969/1969-03-01-batman-s-melbourne-the-wedding-the-greatest-thing-since-the-bogle-case/) — Keith Dunstan covers the Zara Holt wedding at Millicent Avenue, Toorak, a press circus of 62 journalists, live television cameras, uninvited spectators climbing through windows, and the great friesian calf Meadow Glen Dame Zara afflicted with dissipated dyspepsia, all presided over by Nicky Holt in a four-inch tie.
- [There's Gold in Them There Cans for Cats and Canines](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1969/1969-03-08-batman-s-melbourne-theres-gold-in-them-there-cans-for-cats-and-canines/) — The Australian pet food market has more than doubled in three years, with over a million tins sold every week, a fact Keith Dunstan discovers at his supermarket's 30-item dog bar, while witnessing the spectacular launch of Lassie dog food at Le Chateau Restaurant complete with a potted stage musical and a $3000 TV commercial featuring a skateboarding dog.
- [A Reserve Ticket on MacArthur's Bed for Muggeridge](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1969/1969-03-15-batman-s-melbourne-a-reserve-ticket-on-macarthurs-bed-for-muggeridge/) — The four-day auction of the Menzies Hotel's 4000 lots by closed-circuit television, covering twin beds slept in by General MacArthur, Danny Kaye and Sophie Tucker, a $35,000 Czech chandelier, chamber pots with scroll work, the two statues Prudence and Phoebe separated after 102 years, and a bottle of Bass ale from 1902 that nobody thought worth opening for 67 years.
- [Where Culture Reigned and Thunder Rumbled](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1969/1969-03-22-batman-s-melbourne-where-culture-reigned-and-thunder-rumbled/) — The 1969 Moomba festival's bid for culture collapses with a $10,000 balloon that bursts twice, threatening letters and egg-throwing threats against Italian opera star Tito Gobbi as Moomba King, and a Sydney Symphony Orchestra concert attended by fewer people than the ABC's Melbourne typists, while Keith Dunstan reveals that 'moomba' likely means 'thunder' in the Dippil Aboriginal language.
- [The R-R Auction, an Occasion Unique in History](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1969/1969-03-29-batman-roves-again-the-r-r-auction-an-occasion-unique-in-history/) — The estate sale of A. W. Palfreyman's collection of vintage Rolls-Royces at Ingleside, near the Gold Coast, draws collectors from all over Australia by chartered aircraft and personal Bentley, with a 1929 Silver Ghost limousine coach going to Melbourne buyer David Jones for around $6000, and the whole collection fetching $47,000.
- [Thirsting for Spirits in the Theatre](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1969/1969-04-05-batman-s-melbourne-thirsting-for-spirits-in-the-theatre/) — Since Melbourne theatres won the right to apply for liquor licences in 1966 and not one has done so, Keith Dunstan mounts a campaign against the deliberate cruelty of watching four hours of Dylan Thomas drinking himself to death, the entire cast of 'The Season of the Seventeenth Doll' drinking real Carlton beer, and Ray Milland being driven to ruin by the banquet scene in La Traviata.
- [Rolling Along with a Major Revival](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1969/1969-04-12-batman-s-melbourne-rolling-along-with-a-major-revival/) — Keith Dunstan visits the Orchestrelle company in Collins Street to find 1500 pianola rolls from a Toorak estate on sale, and reports on the major revival of player pianos since 1961, with Beatles hits and 'Sound of Music' rolls competing alongside vintage duo-art rolls that reproduce Rubinstein exactly, and one Sydney lady who owns three electric-player grands.
- [On the Wrong Side of Toorak](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1969/1969-04-12-on-the-wrong-side-of-toorak/) — A survey of Toorak's transformation from a hilly suburb of large estates and stately homes into a high-rise battlefield, where Whelan the Wrecker demolishes Sir Robert Knox's neo-Tudor mansion, the Nathan Beller 13-storey flat wins Board of Works approval despite 600 protestors in St. John's Hall, and a Bailey bridge over the Yarra triggers Toorak's first public protest movement.
- [The Kelly Hunt Is On Again](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1969/1969-04-19-batman-s-melbourne-the-kelly-hunt-is-on-again/) — The north-east of Victoria is finally making solid practical use of Ned Kelly as a tourist attraction, with a Kelly corner in Benalla, the recently opened cell under Beechworth courthouse where Kelly was first convicted in 1870, and the Railway Hotel at Glenrowan planning a Kelly museum, while Melbourne's 'Punch' of 1880 recorded 14,805 actual threepenny bits taken from Ned Kelly currently in existence.
- [Kicking Around the Idea of a Footy Supermarket](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1969/1969-04-26-batman-s-melbourne-kicking-around-the-idea-of-a-footy-supermarket/) — The Victorian Football League's 1930 Coulter Law forbids the sale of players while the trade goes on regardless, North Melbourne reportedly paying $2000 for a Box Hill centreman, leading Keith Dunstan to propose a used-footballer market modelled on American baseball, where entire teams are owned by millionaires and Dalgety's could auction the top players.
- [Walkabout Profile: Jean Battersby](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/walkabout-magazine/1969/walkabout-profile/) — A profile of Dr Jean Battersby, newly appointed Executive Director of the Australian Council for the Arts, on subsidising drama, ballet, opera and film, her Sorbonne years on a French government scholarship, and her rejection of the "bricks and concrete" test for judging cultural investment.
- [BHP Leads the High-Rise Trend](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1969/1969-05-03-batman-s-melbourne-bhp-leads-the-high-rise-trend/) — BHP unveils its planned 41-storey tower on the Menzies Hotel site, designed by architect Barry Patten as a severe black-glass building in formal dark suit to contrast with the Hawaiian-shirt towers around it, with a heliport on the roof and natural gas providing a total energy system, part of the greatest wave of high-rise building Melbourne has ever seen.
- [Italy in Suburbia](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1969/1969-05-03-italy-in-suburbia/) — Melbourne has become one of the major Italian cities of the world, with 200,000 first- and second-generation Italians, over 500 Continental delicatessens, Italian-language cinemas in Footscray and Ascot Vale, and an estimated one million gallons of home-made wine produced annually in backyards from Carlton to Reservoir from grenache and muscatel grapes trucked from the Murray.
- [But Will Squizzy's Re-Run Be a Long Run?](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1969/1969-05-10-batman-s-melbourne-but-will-squizzys-re-run-be-a-long-run/) — Nigel Buesst's $2000 documentary film on Squizzy Taylor opens at the Carlton cinema, drawing on old photographs, cartoons, and interviews to portray Theodore Joseph Leslie Taylor as a blackguard, flashy dresser, and public-relations genius who outwitted Melbourne police for ten years before dying in a 1927 gunfight with Sydney criminal John D. Cutmore.
- [Going to Market About an Adopted Young American](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1969/1969-05-17-batman-s-melbourne-going-to-market-about-an-adopted-young-american/) — East Burwood's new K-Mart, the first Australian outpost of the American Kresge Company's discount chain, opens to 5000 customers on its first morning, offering 50 departments and 40,000 items under one vast roof, complete with no-frills pricing, buzzer-controlled lavatories, and a smoking ban copied directly from the American originals.
- [Save Matilda — Write a Verse and Earn a Guinea](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1969/1969-05-24-batman-s-melbourne-save-matilda-write-a-verse-and-earn-a-guinea/) — With Australia still without an official national anthem, Keith Dunstan surveys the shortcomings of the four competing songs, 'Advance Australia Fair,' 'God Save the Queen,' 'Song of Australia,' and 'Waltzing Matilda', and launches a reader competition offering a guinea prize for the best new verse added to 'Waltzing Matilda.'
- [A New Religion in the Temples of Hoyts](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1969/1969-05-31-batman-s-melbourne-a-new-religion-in-the-temples-of-hoyts/) — The $4.5 million Hoyts Cinema Centre, opening June 4 with its aluminium spike and Japanese-pagoda silhouette designed by architect Peter Muller under the influence of Frank Lloyd Wright, replaces the splendour of the Hoyts Regent, Melbourne's largest cinema at 3253 seats, whose mighty Wurlitzer organ was sold to a 23-year-old Sydney man for several thousand dollars at its last performance in January.
- [This Ozone by Any Other Name Would Smell More Sweet](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1969/1969-06-07-batman-s-melbourne-this-ozone-by-any-other-name-would-smell-more-sweet/) — Mayor John Staughton's $30,000 promotion campaign to revive St. Kilda's image as a cosmopolitan resort, complete with 4000 colour brochures comparing it favourably to the French Riviera, prompts Keith Dunstan to point out the suburb's unidentifiable patron saint and suggest it needs a new devastating name to rival Surfers Paradise.
- [Middle-Aged and Methodist Amidst the Nakedness](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1969/1969-06-14-batman-s-hair-middle-aged-and-methodist-amidst-the-nakedness/) — The Melbourne opening of the musical Hair, after producer Harry Miller won approval from Chief Secretary Willis to stage it with full nudity intact, prompts Keith Dunstan's report on the audience in fur and chainmail, the show's sex, blasphemy, and four-letter words assessed from a Methodist-raised vantage point, and the aftermath party at the Chevron where Graham Kennedy's gift of a Rolls-Royce was the talk of the night.
- [Paranoia? Call a PAL](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1969/1969-06-21-batman-s-melbourne-paranoia-call-a-pal/) — Melbourne in 1969 has become a city of protests on every conceivable subject, from students hanging an effigy of Sir Henry Bolte in the Treasury Gardens to football fans demanding MCG ticket reform, prompting Keith Dunstan to propose Protest Agency Limited, a for-hire service providing professional demonstrators, effigy-makers, slogan-writers, and a wardrobe department, at penalty rates for scuffles with police.
- [Mining Ballarat's Golden Past](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1969/1969-06-21-mining-ballarat-s-golden-past/) — Ballarat's Sovereign Hill committee, led by architect Ewen Jones and Ballarat Historical Park Association president John Trevenen, is re-creating an 1850s gold-rush village on the site of the old North Normanby mine, where tourists will pan for gold, enter working shafts by candlelight, and watch a ten-head battery crushing rock, with Bentley's Hotel from the Eureka uprising destined to be the centrepiece.
- [Where the Aim Is Big and the Licence Longest](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1969/1969-06-28-batman-in-the-snow-where-the-aim-is-big-and-the-licence-longest/) — A Queen's Birthday weekend visit to Thredbo, the $44 million Lend Lease ski resort developed by G. J. Dusseldorp in the New South Wales Snowy Mountains, finds wall-to-wall carpet, heated swimming pools, R-and-R packages for Vietnam servicemen, and an Alpine Hotel holding the only liquor licence on the mountain, positioned so that everyone must funnel through it to reach the chairlift.
- [Mirror, Mirror on the Wall, Who's the Most Perverted of Us All?](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1969/1969-07-05-batman-s-melbourne-mirror-mirror-on-the-wall-whos-the-most-perverted-of-us-all/) — Melbourne's Vice Squad charges the cast of Boys in the Band with obscene language and the Customs Minister Senator Scott bans Stig Bjorkman's film 'I Love, You Love,' provoking a film-festival seminar at the Palais Theatre where psychologist John Cowl, novelist David Martin, and broadcaster Corinne Kirby argue that obscene material does not corrupt and that the real censorship problem is Australia's broader pattern of repression.
- [The Red Baron Goes to Battle Again](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1969/1969-07-12-batman-s-melbourne-the-red-baron-goes-to-battle-again/) — The Anti-Football League's latest campaign enlists Robert Joyce's skywriting plane, the Red Baron, to write the AFL battle cube and the letters AFL in half-mile smoke at 12,000ft above Melbourne's six simultaneous football grounds, only for the 50-knot wind to carry the message out beyond Dandenong to be seen by sand-belt golfers rather than MCG pie-eaters.
- [My Wordy Reunion with the Instant Opinion Machine](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1969/1969-07-19-batman-s-melbourne-my-wordy-reunion-with-the-instant-opinion-machine/) — Malcolm Muggeridge visits Melbourne to commune with Barry Jones and Hector Crawford, dispensing opinions at his customary rate, Australia is doomed, California and Scandinavia are both like hell, Parliament will be killed by television, while the vegetarian ascetic finds unexpected rapport with fellow non-drinker Barry Jones, though neither can warm to Marshall McLuhan.
- [If You Can't Beat Them in the Search, Join Me in Research](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1969/1969-07-26-batman-s-melbourne-if-you-cant-beat-them-in-the-search-join-me-in-research/) — The arrival of Hong Kong flu prompts Keith Dunstan's Batman White Paper on the winter disease, tracing its escalating nomenclature from Asian flu through Russian flu to the present, noting research scientists' consistent inability to find a cure, and contrasting their diffidence with the supreme confidence of Mrs. Beeton and the 1836 'Magazine of Domestic Economy,' whose cures involved turpentine flannels, garden snails, and stream frogs.
- [High Living in an Air-Conditioned Ice-Cube Tray](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1969/1969-08-02-batman-s-melbourne-high-living-in-an-air-conditioned-ice-cube-tray/) — Three own-your-own apartment towers planned for Melbourne's city centre, including the almost-complete 17-floor Park Tower at 201 Spring Street, revive an Edwardian tradition of wealthy squatters keeping a city seat, now offered with natural-gas heating, a ceramic fountain in the lobby, and a $100,000 penthouse looking down on St. Patrick's Cathedral with a private rear door for tradesmen.
- [Could Enzymes Lift That Veil off Dull Elections?](https://keithdunstan.org/articles/bulletin/1969/1969-08-09-batman-s-melbourne-could-enzymes-lift-that-veil-off-dull-elections/) — The proliferation of mystery ingredients in household products, Puradent, Hexachlorophene, Gardol, Enzolve, Politogene, leads Keith Dunstan to propose that the Labor, Country, and Liberal parties adopt the same scientific marketing language for the coming election, with Politogene, deep-acting enzymes, and OK-100-15 as their respective selling points.
